deck.request: Show one worked page of every form the worked deck does not use: can Northvale Rail reach 60 million journeys a year by FY31, and how?
deck.brief: One worked page for each page-type form that examples/page-types.pages.json does not draw, on the same fictional regional rail operator, Northvale Rail. Each page stands alone - it compiles, composes and passes the page gates as the only page of a deck - and is printed by `author-deck.mjs --example <type>/<form>`. The file is a catalogue, not a deck to build. Every number is illustrative.
deck.question: Can Northvale Rail grow from 48 million to 60 million journeys a year by FY31, and how?
deck.answer: Northvale can reach 60 million journeys by FY31 by filling the off-peak rather than the full peak: add off-peak frequency first, electrify the Eastern line next and reform fares last.

pages.title: Season tickets never came back; day tickets carry the recovery
pages.rail: Season tickets carried 21.5 million journeys in FY20 and 12.4 million in FY26. Day and advance tickets filled the gap, so the revenue now depends on trips people choose week by week, which a better off-peak timetable can win and a poor one can lose.

annotations.text: Day returns are now 47% of journeys

pages.adds: The points say why punctuality fell with the added service and where the plan gets the margin back
pages.title: Punctuality slipped three points as train-km returned to its peak

points.lead: The network fills before it fails
points.text: Punctuality fell three points while train-km rose from 15.4 million to 18.2 million, because the added trains share the same two-track approach into Leeds. Each late train now delays the one behind it, which did not happen when the timetable had gaps.

The Eastern line runs at 86.1%, the weakest on the network, and its diesel units account for half of all fleet failures. Electric trains from 2030 remove those failures, which is how the plan adds a fifth more service and still holds the 90% floor.

points.lead: What the plan must not do
points.text: Adding off-peak trains before the depot extension opens would park units on running lines overnight and cost another point. The timetable change therefore waits for the twelve new sidings in December 2027.

pages.adds: The points say how much of the gain is new travel and what the trial did not test
pages.title: Every trial route gained off-peak journeys; Skipton gained most

points.text: The six routes that moved to a half-hourly off-peak service gained between 16% and 41% in two years, and Leeds to Skipton gained most because its hourly train had been the fullest. No trial route lost journeys, and the hourly routes beside them grew by 4% over the same period.

Surveys on the trial trains found that one journey in five had moved from the peak; the rest were trips not made by rail before. The trial ran on lines with spare units, so it says nothing about the Coast line, where the fleet is committed until 2030.

pages.adds: The points say which misses matter for the plan and which do not
pages.title: Five of eight operating measures missed target in FY26, punctuality furthest

points.text: Five of the eight measures fell short, and punctuality and fleet availability, the two furthest from target, share one cause: the Eastern line diesel units, which fail three times as often as the rest of the fleet.

Cost per train-km and the customer score beat target, and revenue per journey is within a point of it. The plan therefore starts from an operation that is short of trains that work, not short of money or goodwill.

exhibit.heading: Journeys by line and time of travel, FY26

points.text: The City line carries 19.6 million of the 48.3 million journeys, and two thirds of them in the peak, where its trains are full. Growth there needs longer trains or more track, which the plan does not buy before FY31.

The Eastern and Coast lines together carry 3.2 million off-peak journeys on 11.5 million in total, the thinnest off-peak share on the network. Those two lines are where a half-hourly timetable has the most empty seats to fill.

pages.title: Forty-two of a hundred drivers name the wait, not the fare
pages.rail: The wait for the next train is named by 42 of the 100 drivers surveyed and the fare by 21. A timetable change addresses twice as many of them as a fare cut would, and it costs the operator less for each trip it wins.

pages.title: Three packages take four fifths of the capital programme

points.text: Overhead wires, the depot and fleet, and the power supply come to £520 million of the £640 million. Two of the three belong to electrification, which is why its dates decide when most of the money is spent.

Stations work of £45 million follows the housing sites and can slip a year without touching the timetable. The depot cannot: the half-hourly service needs its twelve sidings before the first added train runs in December 2027.

pages.title: Over half of off-peak seats run empty across the network

points.text: Off-peak trains ran with 54% of their seat-km empty in FY26. The track, the crew and the fuel were paid for whether or not the seats were used, so a passenger in one of them costs nothing extra to carry.

points.lead: Why it is the first lever
points.text: Filling a tenth of those seats adds 1.9 million journeys with no new train. That is why the plan starts with the off-peak timetable and leaves the full peak for the electric fleet.

pages.title: A timetable change needs four approvals, two of them in parallel

points.text: The path offer and the crew plan start from the same bid and run side by side for about fourteen weeks. Whichever finishes later sets the date of the safety case, and so far it has been the crew plan on every change.
A bid lodged after June 2027 misses the December 2027 timetable and waits for May 2028. Every other date in the Dales plan is set backwards from that bid.
The safety case cannot start until both branches report, so a late crew plan delays a path offer that was ready. Starting the crew plan four weeks before the bid removes that wait.

exhibit.root: Can Northvale reach 60 million journeys a year by FY31, and where does the growth come from?

conclusions.text: Not in the peak: trains run above 90% full on all five lines
Between the peaks: over half of off-peak seats run empty

conclusions.text: Half-hourly stations grew off-peak journeys 16.5% in three years
Drivers name the wait for a train twice as often as the fare

settles.what: the four steps of the Dales timetable change and what is true after each

pages.adds: The points put a number on each part and say where the mechanism breaks
pages.title: Four steps take the Dales line from hourly to half-hourly

items.label: Recruit crews
items.text: 36 drivers and guards in post by March 2027

items.label: Extend the depot
items.text: Twelve sidings open by November 2027

items.label: Win the paths
items.text: Timetable bid accepted in the June 2027 round

items.label: Run the service
items.text: Half-hourly off-peak from December 2027

points.text: Training a driver takes eleven months, longer than any other step, so recruitment started in 2026. Two of the three intakes are already in post and the third begins in January 2027.
The added trains need somewhere to stand overnight. Without the twelve new sidings, units would be stabled on running lines and the first morning trains would start late.
Paths are allocated twice a year. A bid accepted in June 2027 puts the service in the December timetable; one that misses it waits until May 2028 and costs 0.9 million journeys.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator

pages.why: The ambition, the levers that deliver it and what they stand on are a structure, and the reader should see which part carries which

settles.what: how the ambition, the three levers and the enabling programme fit together

pages.adds: The points put a number on each part and say where the mechanism breaks
pages.title: The plan rests on three levers and one enabling programme

exhibit.roof: 60 million journeys a year by FY31

pillars.title: Off-peak timetable
points: Half-hourly on the Dales and Valley lines
Units and crews released from the peak

pillars.title: Electrification
points: Overhead wires from Leeds to Hull
Eleven diesel units freed for other lines

pillars.title: Fares and housing
points: Off-peak day returns on every line

exhibit.foundation: Depot extension, 36 more crew and the 2029 power upgrade

points.text: The timetable adds 5.1 million journeys, electrification 3.8 million and fares with housing 2.8 million. Together they take 48.3 million journeys to 60 million, and the timetable alone delivers over two fifths of the gain, which is why it carries the first two years of the plan.

None of the levers works without the foundation: the depot holds the added trains overnight, the crews run them and the power upgrade feeds the wires. A slip in the foundation moves every date above it, so the programme board reviews those three items first each month.

The timetable needs only the depot and the crews, so it starts in December 2027. Electrification waits for the power upgrade in 2029, and fare reform follows once a year of the new timetable has shown how people travel and which tickets they buy.

pages.source: Source: illustrative data for a fictional operator

pages.why: The costs stack from fixed to variable, and which layer a decision touches is the point, so they are drawn as layers

settles.what: the four layers of operating cost per train-km and what moves each

pages.adds: The points put a number on each part and say where the mechanism breaks
pages.title: Four layers of cost sit under every train-km operated

layers.label: Variable: fuel and crew hours
layers.text: £6.10 per train-km; the only layer an added off-peak train incurs, and the one electric traction cuts by 40%

layers.label: Semi-fixed: fleet and maintenance
layers.text: £4.20 per train-km; set by how many units are owned, so it falls when the diesel fleet is retired

layers.label: Fixed: track access
layers.text: £4.10 per train-km; charged by the infrastructure manager whether or not the paths are used

layers.label: Fixed: stations and overheads
layers.text: £3.20 per train-km; staff, buildings and systems that every journey shares

points.text: An added off-peak train uses units and track that are already paid for, so it adds only the variable layer of £6.10 a train-km. That is a third of the average cost of £17.60, which is why it pays back within 26 months.

Electric trains cut fuel by 40% and need less maintenance, so the top two layers both fall on the Eastern line, from £21.40 a train-km to £15.80. Spreading the fixed layers over a fifth more train-km takes the network average to £16.40.

pages.adds: The points put a number on each part and say where the mechanism breaks
pages.title: Four bodies share the timetable; the infrastructure manager sits between them

nodes.label: Northvale Rail
nodes.body: Bids for paths and runs trains

points.lead: Every path goes through one body
points.text: The infrastructure manager allocates paths to passenger and freight operators alike, so a half-hourly Dales service is a request to it, not a decision Northvale can take alone.
Six freight paths a day cross the Dales line between the peaks. Two have not been used since 2024, and the bid asks for those two rather than for new capacity.
The regulator approves access rights only for services the transport authority has agreed to fund, so the two approvals are sought in one submission in March 2027.

pages.adds: The points put a number on each part and say where the mechanism breaks
pages.title: Of 100 car trips in the corridor, eleven could move to rail

stages.label: Start and end near a station

points.text: Only 46 of every 100 car trips in the Dales corridor start and end within a mile of a station. The other 54 are out of reach of any timetable and are not counted in the plan.

points.lead: The wait is the largest loss the plan controls
points.text: Of 29 off-peak trips near stations, only 14 would face a wait under 20 minutes today. A half-hourly service brings that to 27, nearly doubling the trips that can switch.
Eleven of the 14 would switch at the present fare, so price removes three trips where the wait removes fifteen. The fare reform is therefore sequenced last.

pages.title: Most new off-peak journeys come from the car, not from the peak

points.text: Of every 100 journeys the trial added, 48 replaced a car trip and 32 were trips nobody made before. Only 20 moved from the peak, so the trial grew the market rather than rearranging it.
Day returns took 58 of the 100, most of them bought by former drivers on the day of travel. That is the ticket a walk-up half-hourly service suits, and it earns the highest fare per journey.

points.lead: The peak shift is useful too
points.text: The 20 journeys that left the peak freed seats on the fullest trains and went mostly to flexible seasons, the product the 2030 fare reform extends to every line.

points.text: The empty off-peak seats and the Dales crews are both in hand today, which is why the first lever needs no new trains and no outside approval beyond the timetable bid.
The Eastern fleet's failures and the Coast line's missing units have the same cure: electric trains in 2030 release eleven diesel units, enough to cover both.

pages.title: The timetable is the one lever that is both large and quick

points.lead: One lever in the top right
points.text: The off-peak timetable adds 5.1 million journeys and starts in December 2027, eighteen months before anything else of its size. No other lever is both large and quick.
It adds 3.8 million journeys but not before the second half of 2030, and it is the only lever that depends on someone else's work, the 2029 power upgrade.
Later last trains add 0.3 million journeys within a year for almost no capital. They ride on the timetable change and are bid for in the same round.

pages.title: Northvale sits nearer a commuter railway than the plan needs

points.text: Ticket sales have already moved most of the way to pay-as-you-go, with day and advance tickets now 74% of journeys. The timetable has not followed: it is still built around two peaks.

points.lead: Frequency is the gap to close
points.text: Three of five lines run hourly between the peaks. Moving them to half-hourly shifts the operator past the midpoint on frequency, the dimension passengers score lowest.
Only the City line is electric today. The Eastern line joins it in 2030, which takes electric running from a fifth of train-km to a half.

points.text: The draft timetable was agreed in March 2026 and the crew and fleet plan in August, both on their dates. The plan shows the Dales service needs 36 crew and no extra units.

points.lead: The path request is the live step
points.text: The request goes to the infrastructure manager in the June 2027 round. It asks for two unused freight paths, which is why it is expected to be granted without a capacity study.
The safety case takes ten weeks once paths are offered, and the timetable is published twelve weeks before it starts. Neither can be shortened, so the request date sets the start date.

points.lead: The first two phases need no one else
points.text: Preparing and filling the off-peak depend only on the depot, the crews and a timetable bid, all within the operator's control. Their added trains pay back within 26 months, which supports the borrowing for electrification.

points.lead: Phase three is the large bet
points.text: Electrification takes £390 million and depends on a power upgrade outside the operator's control. It is sequenced third so that a slip delays a third of the journeys, not all of them.

points.lead: Phase four needs a year of data
points.text: Fare reform waits until the new timetable has run for twelve months, because the products are designed around how people then travel. The housing sites open in the same years and are served by trains already running.

pages.title: Two lines are ready and worth growing; one is neither

points.text: The Dales and Valley lines have both the empty seats and the units, crews and paths to fill them. Their timetables change in December 2027 and May 2028.
The Eastern and Coast lines have the headroom but not the fleet. Electric trains in 2030 release the eleven diesel units that move them to the right.
The City line is ready but has the least headroom, since its off-peak trains are already the fullest. Its timetable is left as it is until FY31.

pages.title: Halifax and Huddersfield rose to the top on off-peak growth

points.text: Halifax ranked fifth on off-peak growth in FY23 and first by FY25, and Huddersfield rose from sixth to third. Both followed the Valley line's half-hourly timetable, introduced in May 2023, by one year.
Half-hourly since early 2023, Skipton led for two years and ranks second since. The three stations at the top are the three with a train every half hour between the peaks.

Scarborough and Hull, the ends of the Coast and Eastern lines, have ranked seventh and eighth in all four years, on hourly timetables that have not changed since FY23 and with no spare units to change them before 2030.

pages.title: Five dates carry the plan; only the power upgrade is not ours

items.label: Crews recruited
items.text: Thirty-six drivers and guards are in post after three training intakes, enough to run a train every half hour.

items.label: Timetable bid lodged
items.text: The bid asks for two unused freight paths between the peaks, so it needs no capacity study.

items.label: Dales service starts
items.text: A half-hourly off-peak service runs from Leeds to Skipton, with a later last train home.

items.label: Power upgrade delivered
items.text: The network operator energises the grid connection for the Eastern line.

items.label: Electric trains run
items.text: Fourteen electric trains replace the diesel fleet between Leeds and Hull and free eleven units.

points.lead: Three dates are the operator's own
points.text: The crews, the bid and the Dales service depend on nobody else, and each has a named owner. A slip in any of them moves the start by one timetable round, which is six months.
The grid connection is the only milestone the plan cannot recover by working faster. A year's delay costs a third of the plan, so the bi-mode order is held as the fallback.
The Dales service adds 2.4 million journeys a year and the electric trains 3.8 million, so a missed bid costs far less than late wires.

pages.adds: The points say why the stages come in this order and which one carries the risk
pages.title: Six stages take the plan from recruitment to 60 million journeys

items.label: Prepare
items.text: Train 36 crew, extend the depot by twelve sidings and lodge the Dales timetable bid.

items.label: Fill the Dales
items.text: Run a half-hourly off-peak service from December 2027, with a later last train from Skipton.

items.label: Fill the Valley
items.text: Bring Halifax and Huddersfield to the same pattern once the Halifax sidings are extended.

items.label: Electrify
items.text: Energise the Eastern line after the 2029 power upgrade and replace its diesel fleet.

items.label: Reform fares
items.text: Launch flexible season tickets and off-peak day returns on every line.

items.label: Serve new homes
items.text: Open the four station housing sites, served by trains already running.

points.text: The first three stages need only crews, sidings and a timetable bid, all within the operator's control, and their added trains pay back within 26 months. That revenue is what supports the borrowing for the fourth stage.

points.lead: The fourth stage is the bet
points.text: Electrification takes £390 million and waits on a power upgrade the operator does not control. Placed fourth, a slip delays a third of the journeys and leaves the timetable gains untouched.
Fare reform follows a full year of the new timetable, because the products are designed around how people then travel. Launched earlier, it would price a service that passengers had not yet seen.

points.text: The plan fills the 54% of off-peak seats that run empty, and it does so with the fleet it has: the half-hourly timetable uses units that stand idle between the peaks. Journeys rise to 60 million without the unit count changing before 2030.

Electric trains then replace the oldest diesel units on the Eastern line, which frees eleven for the Coast line and takes the cost of a train-km down to £16.40. Punctuality is held at its 90% floor throughout, because the added trains run when the track is free.

pages.adds: The points say what the four numbers mean together for the order of the levers
pages.title: Drivers name the wait twice as often as the fare

items.text: name the wait for the next train as their main reason for driving
name the fare as their main reason
would take the train weekly with a service every half hour
did not know their station's off-peak fare
is the longest wait most would accept without checking a timetable

points.text: The wait is named by twice as many drivers as the fare, so a timetable change addresses more of them than a fare cut and costs less for each trip it wins. That is why the half-hourly service comes first and fare reform last.

points.lead: The demand is stated, not assumed
points.text: One in four drivers says a half-hourly train would get them out of the car once a week. Applied to the corridor's off-peak car trips, that is 1.4 million journeys a year, close to what the trial stations added.

Two thirds did not know the off-peak fare, so a cut would go unnoticed by most of the people it is aimed at. The 2030 reform therefore starts with simpler products rather than lower prices, and it is measured on how many drivers can name the fare a year later.

pages.title: Four priorities decide every trade-off in the plan

items.title: Fill before build
items.text: Use the seats and paths that exist before buying new ones

items.title: Hold the 90% floor
items.text: No added train may cost the network its punctuality

items.title: Fund from fares
items.text: Each phase is paid for by the revenue of the one before

items.title: One owner per lever
items.text: Every milestone has a name against it from the first month

points.text: Fill before build puts the off-peak timetable ahead of electrification: it sells seats that already run empty, while the wires need £390 million before they carry a passenger. Holding the punctuality floor keeps the peak timetable as it is, since every train added there has cost a point.

When the depot extension and the station works competed for the FY27 budget, funding from fares decided it: the depot unlocks 5.1 million journeys within a year and the stations do not. The owner of each lever accepted the order because the rule was agreed before the budget was.

points.text: All eight are regional operators carrying 20 to 70 million journeys a year on mixed commuter and leisure routes, so differences in their off-peak share are not differences of scale or market. Northvale sits sixth of the eight on that share, at 36%.

Westmoor and Tideway moved to a half-hourly off-peak timetable in 2022 and now carry 48% and 46% of their journeys off-peak. Fenland is the peer for electrification: its unit costs fell 24% in the three years after its wires were energised.

points.text: Each of the three added off-peak trains before it changed a fare, and each gained between five and nine points of off-peak share within three years. None of them bought a train to do it: the units already stood idle between the peaks.

Northvale's 36% off-peak share is where Westmoor's was in 2021, on a network of similar size and with the same spare units between the peaks. The plan assumes it gains what Tideway gained, seven points, and treats Westmoor's nine as the upside.

pages.adds: The points say what the landscape means for demand and for the timetable
pages.title: The Dales draw walkers who decide the day before they travel

points.text: Four in five Saturday passengers on the Dales line are making a leisure trip, most of them to walk. They choose the day when the forecast is known, so they buy on the day and cannot be won with advance fares.
A train every half hour out in the morning and a later one home: the last train leaves Skipton at 18:40, before most walks finish, and a trip that returns by car is often made by car the next time.
Saturday departures from Leeds between 09:00 and 11:00 run 88% to 97% full, fuller than the weekday peak, while the trains after 16:00 leave three quarters of their seats empty in both directions.

points.lead: Why it matters to the plan
points.text: The Dales line is the first to move to a half-hourly timetable, in December 2027. Its leisure market responds fastest to frequency, and it is the one line where the units, the crews and the paths are all already in hand.
